## Project Overview

This report details a time series forecasting project designed to predict daily
cyclist volumes on Johnston St. Bridge in Victoria, BC. The pipeline executes data preparation, model training, validation backtesting, and true out-of-sample forecasting for 30 
days in November 2025.

### Victoria's Critical Active Transportation Artery
* The **Johnson Street Bridge** serves as a vital multi-use link connecting downtown Victoria with regional trail networks.
* **Objective:** Build an end-to-end predictive pipeline to forecast daily cyclist volumes.
* **Business Value:** Empower infrastructure management to optimize seasonal maintenance windows and accurately evaluate environmental transit ROI.

## Backtesting

In time series forecasting, we can’t rely on a standard train-test split where you randomly shuffle your data. Because time has a strict direction, shuffling would let your model "peek into the future" to predict the past, known as data leakage.

That is where backtesting comes in. It is the process of testing a forecasting model's predictive accuracy by simulating how it would have performed historically using actual past data.

It is a critical step in time series analysis, as it allows us to evaluate the model's performance on unseen data and ensure that it generalizes well to future observations. While a model that backtests well is not guaranteed to perform well in the future, it is a strong indicator of its potential effectiveness.

Additionally, it helps prevent overfitting, as we can assess how well the model captures underlying patterns without being overly influenced by noise in the training data.



### Evaluating Forecasts

How did the models preform? This is answered with a battery of metrics. We should
not put too much stake in any single metric, but take into account all of our metrics.

If we consider the task of forecasting as if we were medical doctors, metrics are just symptoms of the model's health (performance), and we need to factor several symptoms (metrics) together to get a holistic diagnosis of the model's health (performance). We combine these evaluation metrics with our diagnostic
testing for model assumptions to get a complete picture of model health.

The metrics we will use are:

Mean Absolute Error (MAE) measures the average magnitude of the errors in a set of forecasts, without considering their direction. It is the average of the absolute differences between the actual values ($y_t$) and predicted values ($\hat{y}_t$). The formula for MAE is: 

$$MAE = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} |y_t - \hat{y}_t|$$

This treats all erros linearly, meaning that an error of say 50 cyclists is considered twice as bad as an error of 25 cyclists.

One benefit is that we are using the exact units as the original data, which makes it easy to interpret. However, it does not penalize larger errors more than smaller ones. So, if our model is way off when there is lots of rain, we don't penalize that specifically.


Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) squares the errors before averaging them, and then takes the square root of the final result.

$$RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} (y_t - \hat{y}_t)^2}$$
The Intuition: Because the errors are squared before they are averaged, RMSE puts a much heavier penalty on large errors. An error of 10 results in a penalty of 100, while an error of 5 is only 25.

Like MAE, it expresses the error in the original data units. However, it heavily penalize large, systemic misses or unexpected spikes. If our MAE is better than our RMSE, it indicates that we have a few large misses that are dragging down our RMSE.

A single massive outlier during an unusual event (like a holiday or a sudden data anomaly) can skew the RMSE upward, making a generally excellent model look terrible.

Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) solves the scale problem by expressing the error as a percentage of the actual values. Rather than looking at nominal values, it looks at relative values. It is the average of the absolute percentage differences between the actual values ($y_t$) and predicted values ($\hat{y}_t$). 

$$MAPE = \frac{100\%}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left| \frac{y_t - \hat{y}_t}{y_t} \right|$$
This gives an idea about how far off we are, on average. Being off by 10 units when the actual value is 100 (10% error) is treated the same as being off by 100 units when the actual value is 1,000.

This is a very intuitive metric, since being off by 10% on average gives a better clue than 10 units. It also lets you compare model performance across entirely different time series with different scales.

The division by $y_t$ is scary, since if our observations are close to 0, we can get a huge error. We also
need to make sure that $y_t$ is never 0, since we can't divide by 0. In our case, we are safe, since we have no days with 0 cyclists.


### How did the models perform?


The out-of-sample evaluation metrics for the three models are summarized in the table below. The metrics are calculated based on the forecasts made for November 2025, comparing the predicted cyclist volumes against the actual observed values.

```{r}

#| echo: false
#| include: false

library(gt)
library(dplyr)

# Convert the matrix into a clean dataframe for table formatting[cite: 5]
metrics_df <- as.data.frame(final_metrics) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "Model Architecture")

# Create a professional HTML table
metrics_df %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "November 2025 Production Evaluation Results",
    subtitle = "Johnson Street Bridge Daily Cyclist Volume Forecasts"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(MAE, RMSE),
    decimals = 2
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = MAPE,
    decimals = 2,
    pattern = "{x}%"
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    column_labels.background.color = "#f8f9fa", # 🔥 Fixed the argument name here
    heading.title.font.size = px(18)
  )
```


Across all three metrics, XGBoost outperformed both the OLS and ARIMAX models. 
The RMSE of 285.63 is quite close to its MAE of 233.18, suggesting that isn't prone
to extreme misses. With an MAPE of just under 15%, it indicates that the model's predictions are, on average, within 15% of the actual observed cyclist volumes. Considering the forecasting window of 30 days,
this should be considered quite accurate. 

The ARIMAX model, while performing better than OLS, still lagged behind XGBoost, indicating that the inclusion of exogenous variables alone was not sufficient to achieve optimal forecasting accuracy.

One important note with this sort of open forecasting, where we depend on a forecast
for one or more of our independent variables such as weather, it that the accuraccy 
of each model is contingent on the accuracy of the forecasts for those independent variables. If the weather forecast is off, then our cyclist volume forecast will also be off. This is a limitation of any model that relies on exogenous inputs.


Now consider how close the forecasts were between XGBoost and OLS.


```{r}

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = date, y = Cyclists, group = Model)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = Model, linetype = Model, size = Model)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Actual" = "black", "OLS" = "blue", "XGBoost" = "darkgreen", "ARIMAX" = "red")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Actual" = "solid", "OLS" = "dotdash", "XGBoost" = "dashed", "ARIMAX" = "dashed")) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c("Actual" = 1.2, "OLS" = 0.8, "XGBoost" = 1, "ARIMAX" = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Forecast Evaluation: Actual vs Predicted Cyclist Counts",
    subtitle = "November 2025 Out-of-Sample Model Comparison",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Number of Cyclists"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )
```



Both architectures track the same sudden dips and peaks across the November production window because they share a fundamental reliance on identical exogenous features. Unlike the ARIMAX framework, which derives its momentum from its own historical lags, both OLS and XGBoost evaluate each day based purely on the structural conditions provided to them, such as calendar indicators and daily weather variations. When a sharp weather event or a weekend shift occurs, both models immediately react to the exact same external shocks.

This overlapping behavior strongly suggests that the primary relationships driving daily cyclist volumes are predominantly linear and additive in nature. While XGBoost is a highly flexible and is able to capture non-linear interactions, it will approximate simpler, linear-like step functions if the true underlying data-generating process does not demand high-dimensional complexity.

The fact that XGBoost yields a superior set of evaluation metrics despite looking visually twins with OLS indicates that it is not discovering an entirely separate seasonal trend, but is instead handling the extreme boundaries of the data more effectively. Where the rigid assumptions of OLS cause it to overshoot or over-penalize on volatile days, the tree-based structure of XGBoost keeps its predictions more tightly bounded, capturing subtle thresholds in commuter behavior without losing the shared structural signal.
